newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: ANGER OVER TARDY SPACE PROBE WARNING
Defence Minister, Ian McLachlan, has demanded a rep ort by this afternoon from the Defence Department on the delay in alerting the Prime Minister about a possible threat from the Russian space probe.
The probe crashed to Earth in the Pacific Ocean to the west of Chile, after early fears it would strike northern Australia.
Mr Howard was informed just after eight o'clock yesterday morning, but it's believed Emergency Services Australia, which co-ordinated the salvage operation, knew two hours earlier.
Mr Howard says he'd be angry if it's true that the Defence Department knew before he did.
Mr McLachlan has asked for a report by this afternoon on how the situation unfolded yesterday.
CAREER CHANGE FOR FEDERAL MP
Federal Labor Member for Fraser, John Langmore, is resigning from Parliament to take up a job with the United Nations.
Opposition leader, Kim Beazley, has announced the news in the Federal Caucus meeting.
A spokesman for Mr Langmore says the MP hasn't yet officially resigned from Parliament.
The spokesman says while the fine details are still to be worked out, Mr Langmore won't be resuming his seat when Parliament returns next year.
Mr Langmore will take up the post of Director of the division of Social Development at the UN.
He's been member for Fraser since 1984.
BRYANT WENT TO PORT ARTHUR WELL ARMED
The Supreme Court in Hobart has heard that Port Arthur gunman, Martin Bryant, was well equipped for violence when he left home on April 28th, the day of the shootings.
The court heard Bryant had three firearms, two sets of handcuffs, a sash cord, a hunting knife and a number of cans of petrol with him.
Tasmania's Director of Public Prosecutions, Damien Bugg, told the court Bryant was clearly intent on murderous behaviour when he left for Port Arthur just before ten on the morning of the shootings.
Mr Bugg said Bryant had consumed more alcohol than usual the night before the shootings, and set his alarm for six AM, something his girlfriend said he'd never done before.
The Crown contends Bryant went to the Seascape Guest House when he got to Port Arthur.
About 12.30, a resident heard between six and 12 shots fired.
An hour later, shooting was heard coming from the historic site.
The hearing is continuing.
NEW LAWS TO SPEED UP DEPORTATIONS
New legislation is to be introduced to speed up the process of deporting illegal immigrants.
Prime Minister, John Howard, says the move follows a case brought against the Commonwealth by a group of illegal immigrants, which the boat people won.
The group sued the Government for compensation after being detained for longer than the legal limit of 700 days.
They're to be allowed to stay in Australia, in exchange for smaller compensation payouts, in a deal struck with the Government.
Mr Howard's told Radio 2UE, the Government can't reveal details of the settlement, and was bound by laws passed by the former Labor Government.
SENTENCE FOR CHILD PORNOGRAPHY "TOO WEAK"
The New South Wales government wants to appeal against what it calls a lenient sentence against a teacher who pleaded guilty to possessing child pornography.
Police Minister, Paul Whelan, has asked Police Commissioner, Peter Ryan, to seek urgent legal advice.
Yesterday a 29 year old eastern suburbs school teacher was sentenced to 350 hours of community service with a 500-dollar-a-year good behaviour bond.
Waverley Court heard Jason King had downloaded hundreds of images of children, some as young as seven, from the Internet.
Mr Whelan says the community expects to see people who plead guilty to such crimes receive the appropriate punishment.
OVERHEAD CABLE DEBATE HEATING UP
It's claimed the blight of overhead communications cables and communications towers is generating as much emotion as the euthanasia debate.
Ed Wensing, from the Royal Australian Planning Institute, says the Federal Government has a Constitutional responsibility to resolve the growing unease about overhead cables.
An agreement with the communications companies - Optus, Telstra and Vodaphone - expires next July, and Mr Wensing says it's vital a solution to the problem is found by that time.
He says the current situation caused considerable backlash, with some backbenchers telling him the issue has caused more heartburn than Euthanasia debate.
CALLS FOR THE ABOLITION OF ATSIC
A prominent Aboriginal activist says ATSIC is too centralised and should be scrapped.
Gary Foley was giving the keynote address at a major international indigenous education conference in Toowoomba on Queensland's Darling Downs.
He says ATSIC is an old, notorious and hated department which has been given a few minor cosmetic changes by the government, and then wheeled out as a form of Aboriginal democracy in action
Mr Foley also says there's an element of truth in Independent M.P. Pauline Hanson's comments about an "Aborginal industry".
NETBALL PLAYER FINED
A North Queensland netball player has been ordered to complete 80 hours community service for attacking an umpire.
The Mackay Magistrate's Court has been told umpire Kylie Lay received a broken jaw and other injuries in the assault.
Her mother Mrs Beryl Lay was assaulted as she rushed to her daughter's aid.
Cleaner Grace Hoffman was ordered to complete the community service work and to pay the umpire almost a thousand dollars in compensation.
Solicitor Brian Begg said Hoffman regretted the incident, but became angry and lost her temper when the game was called off.
